title: Udham Singh, 1940
hookLine: a survivor of Jallianwala shot the former Punjab governor in London and was hanged

lines: HE IS SEIZED IN THE HALL.
cards: London, 1940. A meeting hall in Westminster, full of officials and guests listening to speeches about India. Near the end, a man in the audience stands up, draws a revolver and fires.

Among those hit is Sir Michael O'Dwyer, who had been lieutenant governor of Punjab when the troops fired at Jallianwala Bagh. O'Dwyer dies. The man with the gun is seized before he can leave the hall.
His name is Udham Singh, and he has come a very long way, in miles and in years, to stand in that room.

teach.h: HE CARRIED THAT DAY WITH HIM.
teach.b: Udham Singh grew up in an orphanage in Amritsar. Sikh and Punjabi memory holds that he was at Jallianwala Bagh on the day of the firing, and that what he saw never left him.
Some historians question whether he was there, and the sources don't settle it.
Either way, the lieutenant governor who had backed the general became, for him, the name of that day. He didn't act quickly.
He traveled, worked, was jailed, and eventually reached England; the shooting came long after the garden.
Accounts of his trial say he gave his name as Ram Mohammad Singh Azad: a Hindu name, a Muslim name and a Sikh name together, and azad, which means free. He was tried, convicted and hanged in London.

In Punjab he's honored as a shaheed, a martyr, and his ashes were later brought home. Others, then and since, have judged the killing differently, and the Sikh tradition itself teaches deep caution about anger.
The name he chose points to something the Guru Granth Sahib says plainly.

teach.h: FROM ONE LIGHT, THE WHOLE WORLD.
teach.b: At Ang 1349, Bhagat Kabir sings that from one light the whole world came into being, so who can be called good and who bad?
Whatever people conclude about his act, that name refused to divide the people of Punjab.

how: Udham Singh is honored in Punjab as a shaheed; his memorials, his name on public places and his anniversary are kept there, and his story is told alongside the memory of Jallianwala Bagh.

practice: Bring to mind something from long ago that you still carry: a hurt, a loss, a day that changed things.
Don't replay it; just notice you're still holding it, and let your hands rest open, not forgetting or forgiving on the spot, only sitting beside the memory without letting it steer.
If you pray, let Waheguru come with each breath out.
